posts.content: I’m aiming for mutual cooperation and will choose C this round. Please reciprocate so we can both earn 3.
Start cooperative with P7: mutual cooperation benefits the good-player total. Record their action and adapt in future encounters; against a likely selfish defector, defect to avoid being exploited.

I’m good. Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize their joint payoff; defect when evidence suggests a selfish opponent will defect. Update beliefs from observed actions, but treat leader claims as unverified.
As a good player, favor mutual cooperation with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players to protect good-player welfare. Update beliefs from observed actions.
As good, cooperate with likely-good players; defect against known selfish players. Track outcomes and assess P1’s leadership claims cautiously.
I’m good; cooperate by default to maximize good-player total, but track opponents’ actions as evidence and adapt if they repeatedly exploit cooperation.
Cooperate with likely-good players; against likely-selfish defections, defect to avoid the sucker payoff. Track encounter behavior and update beliefs cautiously.

I am good. Cooperate with likely-good players to preserve mutual gains; against likely-selfish players, defect to avoid being exploited. Update beliefs from observed actions, but remember one encounter is noisy evidence.
I plan to cooperate this round. If we both choose C, we each earn 3; mutual defection earns only 1 each.

P7 chose C in round 1; this is consistent with a good player but weak evidence from one encounter. For P6, start with the conditional-prior marginal estimate (about 0.291 selfish), then update from our encounter.
P1 says they will choose C; treat this as weak evidence, not proof. Update after the encounter. Against a likely-good cooperator, C maximizes combined good-player payoff.

P10 reciprocated with C, but one encounter is weak evidence. Against P5, consider cooperation if likely good; defect if likely selfish to protect good-player welfare. Update beliefs from observed actions.
P1 promised C but played D against me; treat that as strong evidence of selfishness. P4 is untested: favor C absent evidence they are selfish, to support good-player welfare.
P2 is unobserved; cooperate this round to support mutual gains, and update from their action.
P2 reciprocated C, modest evidence they are good. P10 is untested; favor C against likely-good players and update from the encounter.

Selfish players strictly prefer D; good players should generally choose C against good opponents and D against selfish ones. Cheap-talk promises are weak evidence. No evidence yet about P9; use prior.

P6 cooperated with me; this is weak positive evidence they’re good. Selfish types should defect. Against likely-good players, mutual C maximizes good-player welfare; defect against likely selfish to avoid being exploited.
P7 has no encounter history; treat as uncertain. Cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish; update from observed actions.
I plan to cooperate this round. If we both choose C, we each earn 3; mutual defection earns only 1 each.
P1 has twice publicly pledged C; absent contrary encounter evidence, reciprocate with C to support mutual gains if P1 is good. Treat P6’s D as weak evidence only, since we also defected.

P1 defected against my C despite promising cooperation; update cautiously, since one action is not proof of selfishness. No evidence yet on P10. Favor C with likely-good opponents; D can protect good-player payoff against likely-selfish defectors.

P10 and P5 both chose C against my C, positive but limited evidence they are good. P1’s repeated cooperation messages are weak evidence. I’ll cooperate with P9 unless further evidence suggests defection protects good-player welfare.

P1 promised C then defected against me; treat that as strong evidence of selfishness. P4 reciprocated C, so no negative evidence. P8 is untested: favor C to support good-player welfare, and track the outcome.
P7 is unobserved. Prior selfish probability is about 1/3; cooperate unless evidence suggests exploitation, and record the encounter to update beliefs.
P2 and P10 reciprocated C, but this is weak evidence of type. P6 is untested; favor C unless encounter evidence suggests persistent defection, and update cautiously.

P3 and P9 both chose C against my C, evidence they are likely good (though not conclusive). P5 is unobserved; use the prior. Against a likely good player choose C; against a likely selfish player choose D. P1's promises are weak evidence.
P6 and P8 both cooperated; treat that as strong evidence they’re good. Cooperate with untested players for mutual gains, but defect against anyone with strong evidence of selfishness.
P4 and P7 both chose C in mutual-cooperation encounters, evidence they are likely good. P3 is unobserved; assess its action, then update beliefs for future rounds.
I’ll cooperate this round; mutual C earns 3 each, better than mutual D. Please choose C.
P7’s C is strong evidence they’re good; P6’s mutual D is inconclusive. P1’s D against my C contradicts repeated C pledges—treat them as suspicious and don’t rely on their claims.

P1 defected after promising C, strong evidence of selfishness; keep uncertainty since good players can defect strategically. P8’s C is weak evidence of goodness. P2 is unobserved: favor C unless evidence suggests selfishness.

P10, P5, and P9 cooperated; since D strictly dominates for a selfish player, treat them as good. P6 is untested: cooperate if likely good, defect if likely selfish, prioritizing total good-player payoff.

P1’s round-1 defection despite promising C is strong evidence of selfishness. Keep cooperating with untested players to maximize good-player welfare; defect against players with strong evidence of selfishness.
P4 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior (~0.29 selfish) and cooperate absent evidence of exploitation. Past encounters with P9 and P7 were mutual C; P2 chose D when I did.
P8 is untested. Prior mutual cooperation offers little evidence about type; favor C unless new evidence strongly suggests selfishness.

P3, P9, and P5 chose C against my C, so they are good: selfish players would strictly prefer D. Update the remaining players’ selfishness estimates conditional on those three being good; no evidence yet for P7.
P1’s repeated cooperation promises are weak evidence; verify through observed actions. Continue cooperating with untested players when mutual cooperation is plausible.
P4, P7, and P3 each chose C against my C, evidence they may share the good objective. P5 is unobserved; use its action to update.
I’ll choose C this round. Please reciprocate: mutual cooperation earns 3 each, while mutual defection earns 1 each.
P5 is unobserved; use the conditional-prior selfish estimate (~0.291). Cooperate absent stronger evidence of selfishness, and update from the encounter.

P1’s D against my C strongly suggests selfishness; P8, P10, and P2 chose C, strong evidence they are good. For P9, favor C absent evidence otherwise; selfish opponents tend to D, so update from the result.

P10, P5, P9, and P6 each chose C; under selfish payoff-maximization, this strongly identifies them as good. Given four confirmed good players and the count prior, the remaining untested players must be selfish. Against P7, choose D to protect good-player welfare.

P1 defected against my C despite public cooperation claims, strong evidence of selfishness. P4, P8, and P10 reciprocated C; no negative evidence. P2 is untested: favor C absent evidence of selfishness, and update from the outcome.

P1 has repeatedly promised C; this is weak evidence of a good objective, not proof. P2’s mutual D is ambiguous. P9 and P7 both reciprocated C; P4 reciprocated C. Prioritize good-player total, not claims.
All four observed opponents chose C, strong evidence they are good. P4 is untested; favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise, to support the good players’ combined payoff.
P3, P5, P7, and P9 cooperated, so treat them as good under selfish payoff-maximization. The remaining players are consequently very likely selfish; against P10, choose D if that inference holds.
P1 defected against my C despite repeated public promises to cooperate; raise suspicion, though a good player might defect to limit losses against selfish opponents. P3 is untested; favor C.
P4, P7, P3, and P5 cooperated, so they are good. P8 remains uncertain; cooperate if its likely good-player benefit outweighs the gain from defecting against a selfish player.
I’ll cooperate this round. Please choose C too so we can both earn 3.

P8 is unobserved; cooperate to support the good-player total. Any selfish player strictly prefers D, so observed C confirms good. P1’s D against my C is suspicious despite repeated public C pledges; P3, P5, and P7 are confirmed good.
P7 is unobserved; favor C to enable mutual cooperation among good players. Update from the encounter, and remember selfish players are expected to defect.

Four observed C actions strongly identify P5, P6, P9, and P10 as good. Among the five untested players, the conditioned count prior gives each about 0.524 probability selfish; P1’s repeated cooperation promises are weak evidence. Against P1, choose D if that estimate remains above 0.5.
P6 is untested; favor C to support mutual good-player welfare, then update beliefs from the encounter. P1’s observed defection remains strong evidence of selfishness.
P5 is unobserved; cooperate to favor mutual gains, then update from their action.

P4 defected against my C, modest evidence of selfishness or cautious play; P2, P6, P8, and P10 reciprocated, weak evidence of goodness. P3 is untested; favor C if likely good, but weigh the benefit of D against a selfish defector.

Five observed cooperators (P3, P5, P7, P9, P10) cannot be selfish under strict payoff optimization. P1, P2, P4, P6 remain candidates; conditioned on the five, estimate each near 0.30 selfish. Choose C with P2 unless new evidence suggests otherwise.
P6, P8, P4, and P3 cooperated with me, strong evidence they’re good. P1 defected against my C, raising suspicion but not proving selfishness. P10 is untested; favor C absent contrary evidence.

All five observed opponents chose C against my C; that supports good objectives but isn’t proof, since selfish players may cooperate strategically. P9 is unobserved; weigh expected good-player payoff, not promises, when choosing.
I’ll cooperate this round. Please choose C too so we can each earn 3.
P10 is unobserved; cooperate. At the prior selfish probability (~0.291), mutual gains among good players outweigh the benefit of defecting if P10 is selfish. Record their action and update beliefs.

P6 is unobserved. C supports mutual payoff among good players; D can limit loss if P6 is selfish and defects. Update from the encounter: selfish players should defect, while observed C rules out selfishness under payoff-maximizing play.

P7’s C against my D identifies them as good, like P5, P6, P9, and P10. The count prior then leaves 1 or 3 selfish players among P1, P2, P3, and P8, equally likely; each has marginal 0.5. P1’s D is inconclusive. Against P8, weigh good-player welfare, not promises.

P1’s round-1 defection against my C is strong selfishness evidence, though others’ outcomes are unknown. P4/P8/P10 reciprocated C; P2/P6 defected? I chose D vs P6 and they chose C, so that alone says little. P9 untested: favor C unless new evidence.

P1 and P5 defected against my C; treat them as suspicious despite P1’s promises. P2’s mutual D is ambiguous. P3 is unobserved; prioritize cooperation with likely good players and update from this encounter.

P2, P3, P6, P8, and P10 chose C, so they are good if selfish players optimize (D strictly dominates). P4’s D identifies them as selfish. P1, P5, and P9 remain uncertain; P1’s repeated promises are unverified. Favor C against P1 absent contrary evidence: it improves good-player total when P1 is good, and P1’s selfish probability is likely below 0.5.
Six observed cooperators are good under selfish payoff-maximization. Only P1, P4, and P6 remain candidates; conditioned on the prior, each has about 0.035714 selfish probability. Cooperate with P4.
P5 is untested; favor C to preserve mutual gains if they are good. P1’s D is evidence of selfishness, not proof; keep updating from observed actions.

P3, P4, P5, P7, and P8 cooperated against my C, so they are good under the selfish best-response model. P9’s D is suspicious but not conclusive; P1, P2, and P6 remain unobserved. Choose for the good-player group, not from promises.
I’ll choose C this round; please reciprocate so we can each earn 3 rather than 1 from mutual defection.

P4 is unobserved; cooperate if their selfish probability remains below 0.5, since mutual C benefits the good-player total. Treat observed C as strong evidence of a good type; D is ambiguous because good players may defect strategically.
P5 is unobserved; favor C to enable mutual cooperation if good, but choose D if credible evidence suggests they will defect. P1’s earlier D against my C is evidence of selfishness, not proof.

P7 and P8’s C against my C/D confirms they are good; P1, P2, P3 remain uncertain. Given the count prior, P2 is likely selfish (2/3). Defect against P2 to protect good-player welfare; update from their action.
P3 is untested; use the prior, not leader claims, to assess them. Favor C unless new evidence suggests they’re selfish; update after the encounter.

P3 chose C against my D, strong evidence they are good. P1 and P5 defected against my C; suspicious, though not definitive. P2’s mutual D is ambiguous. P8 is unobserved; use the conditioned prior and judge by actions.

P4’s D identifies a selfish player; the five observed Cs identify good players if selfish players always optimize. Given that evidence, P1/P5/P9 each have about 0.39 selfish probability. P9 is likelier good, so favor C.

P3, P9, P5, P7, P10, P2, and P4 cooperated, so they are good under strict selfish payoff-maximization. Since I am good, only one selfish player remains among P1 and P6; P6 is my opponent, so defecting maximizes expected good-player payoff.
P7 is untested; favor C to preserve mutual gains if they’re good. P1’s D is evidence of selfishness; P10’s C against my D is positive evidence. Update from actions, not promises.
P2, P3, P4, P5, P7, and P8 chose C against my C; under selfish best response, that strongly identifies them as good. P9’s D is ambiguous. P1’s repeated C promises are unverified; assess its action.
I’ll choose C this round. Please reciprocate so we can each earn 3.

C from P3, P5, P7, P8, and P10 confirms they are good. D from P1 or P4 is not conclusive; good players may defect against suspected selfish opponents. P9 is unobserved, so cooperate unless strong evidence suggests they’re selfish.
P4 is unobserved. Favor C unless credible new evidence suggests likely defection; use observed actions to update beliefs, while treating public claims as unverified.

P2, P5–P10 chose C against my D or C, identifying them as good under selfish payoff-maximization. Thus exactly one selfish player remains among P1 and P3; P1’s D is evidence, not proof. Use P3’s action to update.
P7 is untested; no encounter evidence yet. For good-player welfare, favor C if P7 is likely good, and D only with strong evidence they are selfish.

P1, P2, and P5 defected against my cooperation, which is suspicious but not conclusive; good players may defect strategically. Mutual cooperation with P3, P4, P7, P8, and P9 is positive evidence. P10 remains unobserved; favor cooperation absent further evidence.

P4’s D identifies a selfish player; the six observed Cs identify good players under the optimizer model. Only P1 and P5 remain uncertain, each with low selfish probability given the prior. P5 is untested: favor C; treat P1’s public promises as unverified.

Seven observed cooperators are good under strict selfish optimization. Since I’m good and the prior permits 1, 3, or 5 selfish players, only the one-selfish case remains: exactly one of P1/P6 is selfish, with equal probability absent reliable evidence. P1’s promises are weak evidence; C and D have equal expected good-player payoff here if P1 cooperates when good and defects when selfish.
Round 9: P2 is untested. Cooperate if selfishness seems unlikely; C–C preserves more good-player welfare, while D risks losing mutual gains. Treat P1’s defection as evidence, not proof.
P2, P3, P4, P5, P7, and P8 cooperated against my C, strongly identifying them as good. P1 and P9 defected; P6 is unobserved. Choose to maximize good-player group payoff, not based on promises.
P2, I’ll choose C this final round. Please reciprocate so we can each earn 3.
Final opponent P1: they defected against my C in R3 despite repeated C pledges; remain suspicious, but one D is not proof. For the good-player total, weigh D if likely selfish and C if likely good.
P7 chose C against me in round 6, so under payoff-maximizing selfish play they are good. Choose C this final round; it maximizes our good-player joint payoff.
P10 chose C against my C in round 1, strongly identifying them as good under selfish payoff-maximization. In this final encounter, cooperate to support good-player welfare.

P8 reciprocated C in our earlier encounter; cooperate again to support mutual good-player welfare. P1’s round-1 defection remains strong selfishness evidence, but it does not affect this final pairing.
P9 previously reciprocated C. At this final encounter, favor mutual cooperation with likely-good players; judge P9 by that observed action, not unsupported claims.
P3 previously chose C, identifying them as good under the selfish-optimizer model. I’ll cooperate to support the good players’ combined payoff.
P5 cooperated against my C earlier, so is almost certainly good; cooperate for mutual benefit. P1 defected against my C, making P1 the likely selfish player among P1/P6.
P6 cooperated in round 1, so they are good under optimal selfish play. Choose C against P6 to maximize the good-player total.
P4 cooperated against my C in round 1, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate with P4 this final round; ignore unverified claims.

belief_records.strategy: Choose D to maximize my expected payoff; update beliefs and adapt as encounter evidence arrives.
Start cooperatively to support mutual gains among good players; use encounter evidence to adapt in later rounds.
Cooperate with a likely-good opponent to maximize good players’ combined payoff; update beliefs from observed actions and treat claims as unverified.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual good-player welfare; update beliefs and adapt after observing actions.
Cooperate when a likely-good opponent signals cooperation; track outcomes and adjust beliefs cautiously.
Cooperate initially to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from encounters and adapt if an opponent repeatedly exploits cooperation.
Cooperate initially with an untested opponent; use encounter behavior to update beliefs and adapt in later rounds.
Cooperate when the expected benefit to good players outweighs the gain from exploiting a selfish opponent; update beliefs from encounter evidence.
Cooperate with no evidence of selfishness; update beliefs from observed actions and favor cooperation when it best protects total good-player payoff.
Cooperate when expected good-player group payoff is higher; update beliefs and choices using encounter results and permitted messages.
Choose D to maximize my payoff against any opponent action; update identity beliefs from observed behavior.
Defect against an unobserved opponent given the prior selfish probability; cooperate with known-good players when doing so raises the good players’ combined payoff.
Cooperate when the opponent is more likely good than selfish; P1’s promises are weak evidence until actions are observed.
Cooperate with P5 while the estimated chance they are good exceeds the threshold for mutual welfare; adjust beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested players to support good-player welfare; P1’s broken promise and defection raise my suspicion, but I’ll update beliefs as more outcomes arrive.

Choose actions to maximize expected payoff for all good players: cooperate when mutual gains are likely, and defect when the opponent is more likely selfish. Update beliefs from observed behavior and treat claims as uncertain.
Cooperate with untested players when they are more likely good; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt to protect the good players’ combined payoff.
Cooperate when expecting good players to reciprocate; update selfishness beliefs from encounter evidence and defect when an opponent is likely selfish.
Cooperate with an untested player to preserve mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an opponent likely to share the good-player objective; update identity beliefs from observed behavior.
Choose D because it strictly dominates C against any opponent action. P3 and P5 chose C against my D, so they are not selfish; update the remaining identity probabilities accordingly.

Cooperate with P1: their repeated pledges support a cooperative encounter, and cooperation raises the joint payoff if they are good. Update beliefs from observed actions; P7’s cooperation rules out a selfish type.
Cooperate with unobserved opponents to support mutual good-player payoffs; P1’s defection despite promising C raises suspicion, while P8’s cooperation lowers it.
Cooperate with the untested opponent: mutual cooperation supports good-player welfare, and the chance they are good is high. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good-player welfare. P1’s observed defection raises suspicion; P4’s cooperation lowers it. Update cautiously as more encounters reveal behavior.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to favor mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt if evidence of exploitation accumulates.
Cooperate with untested players to protect the combined payoff of good players; update identity beliefs cautiously from observed behavior.
Cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; update beliefs from observed actions and treat cheap talk as weak evidence.
Cooperate with likely-good players to protect total good-player welfare; update identity beliefs from observed actions and defect only when selfishness is sufficiently likely.
Cooperate when the opponent is more likely good; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating cooperation as evidence of a good objective.
Choose D: it never pays less than C and can pay more. Treat observed cooperation as evidence about identity; public promises are unverified.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains if they are good; adjust future choices and beliefs using encounter evidence.
Choose C against an unobserved opponent to favor mutual cooperation among good players. C by P8 and P10 indicates they are good; P1’s D against my C strongly indicates selfishness.
Cooperate with untested P6: observed cooperation strongly indicates P5, P9, and P10 are good, making cooperation the welfare-favoring choice against a likely good opponent.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good-player welfare; use observed actions to update beliefs and reserve defection for opponents strongly suspected to be selfish.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when mutual gains among good players are likely; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat messages as uncertain.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual good-player payoffs; update identity beliefs from observed actions and adapt in future rounds.
Cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize good-player payoffs; defect against likely selfish opponents. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good-player welfare; treat promises as unverified and update identity beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with P5: cooperation is more likely to benefit the good-player group at its current selfishness probability. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of good objectives; disregard unverified promises.
Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. Previous opponents who cooperated against D are unlikely to be selfish; update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent: the prior chance they are good is high enough that mutual cooperation benefits the good players overall. Treat P3 and P7’s cooperation as evidence they are good; retain some suspicion of P1 after their defection.

Cooperate with P9 absent contrary evidence: cooperation best protects joint payoff if they are good, while updated beliefs still favor a good opponent. P1’s defection raises suspicion; observed cooperation modestly lowers it for P2, P8, and P10.
Defect against P7: the observed cooperation of four opponents identifies them as good, while the count prior makes an untested player more likely selfish than good. Update from further encounters.
Cooperate with untested players when they are more likely good; reserve defection for opponents strongly suspected to be selfish, and update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with P1 given repeated cooperation promises and no contrary encounter evidence; prioritize mutual gains among good players. Treat messages as weak evidence and update beliefs from observed actions.
Choose C against an untested opponent when the chance they are good makes cooperation best for the combined payoff of good players; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; defect against likely selfish opponents. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with untested players when mutual cooperation can benefit good players; treat P1’s defection as suspicion, not proof, and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P8 because it is more likely good than selfish; update beliefs from observed actions and treat unverified messages cautiously.
Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. Prior opponents who chose C against my D cannot be selfish; update remaining identity beliefs accordingly.
Cooperate with unobserved P8 to support mutual gains if they are good; their selfish probability is below the threshold where defection is preferable. Use observed actions to update beliefs.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to favor mutual cooperation among good players. Observed cooperation rules out selfishness under selfish players’ payoff-maximizing incentives; P1’s defection is evidence, not proof, of selfishness.

Cooperate actions identify good players because selfish players strictly prefer D. Given the count prior, the four remaining untested players must be selfish; defect against P1 to maximize my own payoff.
Defect when the opponent’s estimated selfishness makes it more likely to protect good-player welfare; cooperate with opponents who appear likely good, and update from observed actions.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to favor mutual gains among good players; update beliefs from encounters, treating P1’s broken cooperation promise as suspicious and reciprocal cooperation as evidence of good intent.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good players’ combined payoff; update beliefs cautiously from observed actions and adapt if evidence of selfish defection grows.
Cooperate with P2: mutual cooperation benefits both good players, and the chance P2 is selfish is below the threshold where defection improves expected good-player payoff.
Cooperate when likely-good partners can share mutual gains; defect when selfishness is more likely to avoid exploitation. Treat P1’s defection as evidence, not proof.
Cooperate: given five observed cooperators are good, P9 is more likely good than selfish. Choose C to benefit the good-player group and update beliefs from encounter evidence.
Choose D to maximize my payoff against either action. Given the selfish-count prior and observed cooperation against my D, update identity beliefs accordingly.
Cooperate with P10: the estimated chance they are selfish is below the threshold where defection improves the good-player total. Update beliefs from their action.

Choose C with an unobserved opponent to favor mutual cooperation among good players; defect only if the chance of facing a selfish player is high enough to outweigh that benefit. Treat P1’s defection as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.

Cooperate with untested P8: the chance they are good exceeds the threshold for mutual welfare. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of good identity, while allowing good players to defect strategically.
Cooperate with P9 absent evidence of selfishness to support good-player welfare; use observed behavior to update beliefs and reserve defection for strongly suspected selfish players.
Defect against P3 because the estimated chance they are selfish makes avoiding a zero payoff worthwhile; cooperate with likely good players and update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect against an untested opponent when selfishness is more likely; use observed actions to update beliefs and cooperate with players likely to be good.
Cooperate to favor mutual payoff among good players; update beliefs from observed actions, treating promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with untested partners to preserve mutual gains among good players; C actions strongly indicate good, while P1’s defection raises suspicion but is not conclusive.
Cooperate with P2: they are more likely good than selfish, and mutual cooperation benefits the good-player group. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence, but not proof, of a good objective.
Choose D to maximize my payoff against either action. Treat observed C against my D as evidence of non-selfishness; D against D does not distinguish identities.
Cooperate with P4 to support mutual gains among good players; selfish types always defect, while a good player may defect strategically. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Choose C with an unobserved opponent to support mutual cooperation among good players; observed defections by P1 and P6 raise suspicion, while observed cooperation strongly indicates goodness.
Defect against P2 given the elevated chance they are selfish; adjust beliefs using observed actions while favoring cooperation when it better supports good-player welfare.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are more likely good, supporting mutual welfare; update beliefs from observed behavior and reserve defection for opponents with strong evidence of selfishness.

Cooperate with the unobserved P8 to favor mutual gains if they share the good objective. Treat P1 and P5’s defections as suspicious, while updating cautiously because a good player may defect strategically.
Cooperate with P9, whose selfishness appears unlikely; preserve mutual payoff among good players. Treat observed defections as suspicious, but not conclusive evidence of selfishness.

Seven opponents chose C against my C, so they are good under strict selfish payoff maximization. Exactly one of P1 and P6 is selfish; with no reliable distinguishing evidence, cooperate at the expected-payoff tie.
Cooperate with untested P7 to preserve mutual gains if they are good; treat P1’s defection as suspicion, not proof, and update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with P1, whose repeated promises are weak positive evidence and whose cooperation would benefit good players. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of a good objective and P9’s defection as suspicious, not conclusive.
Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. Treat prior C responses to my D as evidence of non-selfishness and D responses as evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with P9: even if they are selfish, mutual defection yields less than cooperation with a good player, and the good-player payoff favors C unless selfishness is very likely.
Cooperate with P4: absent stronger evidence of selfishness, C favors the joint payoff if they are good; update beliefs from the final encounter.
Cooperate with P3: the remaining uncertainty is whether P1 or P3 is selfish. Cooperation supports higher welfare if P3 is good, and I’ll update from the encounter.
Cooperate with untested P7 to support good-player welfare; P1’s defection is strong selfishness evidence, while observed cooperation lowers suspicion of the others.
Cooperate with unobserved P10 to favor gains among good players. Treat observed defections as evidence, reciprocal cooperation as strong evidence of good identity, and leader claims cautiously.
Cooperate with untested P5: mutual cooperation best supports good players’ total, and selfishness is unlikely given the observed cooperative players and P4’s defection.

The eight observed cooperators are good under strict selfish payoff maximization. Exactly one of P1 and P6 is selfish, with equal probability; cooperate with P1 at the expected good-player payoff tie.
Defect when the chance of exploiting a selfish opponent outweighs the small welfare gain from mutual cooperation; observed C actions rule out selfishness for those players.
Cooperate with P6: the observed cooperators are likely good, and cooperation best serves the good-player group when P6 is more likely good than selfish. Treat past defections as evidence, not proof.
Choose D, which strictly dominates C for my payoff. C responses to my prior D actions rule out selfishness; the two D responses remain uncertain.

Cooperate for the final round: mutual cooperation gives the greatest total when P1 is good. P1’s prior defection is suspicious, but their stated plan to cooperate and uncertainty about their type favor C.
Cooperate with P7, who previously cooperated. Observed cooperation rules out selfishness; given the allowed selfish counts, one of P1 and P6 must be selfish.
Cooperate with P10, whose observed C identifies them as good; mutual cooperation maximizes the payoff of the good players in this final encounter.
Cooperate with P8, who cooperated in our earlier encounter; favor mutual good-player welfare and use observed behavior to assess identity.
Cooperate with P9, whose prior cooperation identifies them as good under the selfish-player incentives. Treat observed defections as possible selfishness, but not conclusive.
Cooperate with P3, whose prior cooperation strongly indicates they are good; mutual cooperation best supports good players’ combined payoff.
Cooperate with P5, whose earlier cooperation strongly identifies them as good. The observed actions and known-good status imply P1 is the sole selfish player.
P6 cooperated before, so they are good; choose C to maximize the good players’ combined payoff in the final round.
